metadata.title: Pedagogical practices and civic knowledge and engagement in Latin America: Multilevel analysis using ICCS data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 microdata with a two-stage sampling design (schools, then students/teachers in target grades). For the multilevel HLM estimation, the authors explicitly apply ICCS within-school student weights at level 1 by multiplying class- and student-level weight factors (WGTFAC2S × WGTADJ2S × WGTADJ3S), and apply a school weight at level 2 derived from WGTFAC1 and WGTADJ1S (and WGTFAC1 × WGTADJ1T for teacher-level analyses). They also note that, per ICCS user guidance, weights should be normalized so that the sum of weights equals the sample size, to preserve representativeness under the complex design. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported in the provided text, and the analysis is conducted with HLM8 using the ICCS-recommended weighting approach.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable (SCKE) is based on ICCS cognitive test scaling with five plausible values, but the manuscript does not describe any explicit missing-data handling procedure for questionnaire or test variables. This is a reporting gap because ICCS datasets typically contain missingness in background/attitudinal items, and the analysis uses multilevel models where missingness strategy can affect estimates. The paper therefore provides insufficient transparency to assess whether missingness was handled via imputation, listwise deletion, or other methods.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to five Latin American and Caribbean countries that participated in ICCS 2016 (Chile, Colombia, Peru, Dominican Republic, Mexico). The target student population is 13–14-year-olds in eighth grade (or ninth grade in countries where the average age in eighth grade is below 13.5 years), and the analysis includes the corresponding teachers for those grades. The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., missing covariates, booklet completion, or specific item-level filters) beyond the ICCS multistage design and the use of the ICCS cognitive test SCKE with five plausible values.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 (Grade 8/9) Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE) cognitive test
main_findings.target_variable: Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE; five plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel HLM8 results reported as regression coefficients (b) with t-tests by country; e.g., Colombia: O PDISC b=540, t(54)=4.46, p<.001; Chile: S_CIVLRN b=4.11, t(151)=3.94, p<.001; Peru: O PDISC b=6.43, t(183)=6.41, p<.001; negative associations for S_COMPART in all countries where significant (e.g., Colombia b=-6.06, t(114)=-4.068, p<.001; Peru b=-6.63, t(183)=-5.27, p<.001). No ML accuracy/AUC/R² metrics are reported because the analysis is multilevel regression rather than predictive ML.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 (Grade 8/9) Civic Knowledge and Engagement (SCKE) the study leveraged openness in classroom discussions, civic learning at school, civic participation in the wider community, expected education level, and home literacy resources to model SCKE, finding that civic learning and classroom openness were positively associated with civic knowledge in several countries while civic participation in the wider community showed statistically significant negative associations. This indicates that strengthening in-class civic learning and open classroom discussion practices may improve civic competencies, while encouraging broad community political participation may require careful alignment with students’ academic learning time and support, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This Heliyon study analyzes ICCS 2016 civic outcomes for 13–14-year-olds in five Latin American and Caribbean countries (Chile, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Peru) using the ICCS cognitive test SCKE, which is scaled on a 500 (SD=100) metric and estimated via five plausible values. The authors fit hierarchical linear models (HLM8) to account for the nested school structure and report multilevel regression coefficients (b) with t-tests and p-values by country rather than ML performance metrics (no accuracy/AUC/R²). Across countries, openness in classroom discussions and civic learning at school are associated with higher SCKE in multiple settings (e.g., Colombia and Peru), while civic participation in the wider community is consistently negative where significant (e.g., Colombia b=-6.06; Peru b=-6.63). The study uses ICCS-recommended within-school student weights and school weights, but it does not report a missing-data handling strategy, limiting assessment of robustness. Because the design is cross-sectional, observed associations cannot be interpreted causally.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses multilevel modeling (HLM) with plausible values and survey weights, it does not train or evaluate machine-learning algorithms (no predictive ML model comparison is reported). Therefore, the ML technique fields are left empty and the extraction focuses on the multilevel regression results. The absence of ML metrics (accuracy/AUC/R²) is consistent with the study’s stated analytical approach rather than a reporting omission.
